t.7.26.1: When the sun had reached the western mountain, the mighty Daśagrīva resolved to make his camp there together with his army.
t.7.26.2: When the spotless moon had risen, its radiance equal to that of the mountain, he beheld there the splendid features of the place, made beautiful by the moon's rays.
t.7.26.3: It was graced with heavenly groves of karṇikāra trees and likewise with dense thickets of kadamba, with lotus pools in full bloom, and with the waters of the Mandākinī as well.
t.7.26.4: In the abode of Dhanada was heard the sweet-toned sound of the throngs of Apsaras hosts as they sang, like the ringing of bells.
t.7.26.5: The trees, struck by the wind and showering down rains of blossoms, fragrant with the scents of the spring months Madhu and Mādhava, seemed to perfume that mountain.
t.7.26.6: A pleasant breeze blew, bearing an abundant fragrance mingled with the pollen of spring blossoms, and kindled ever more the desire of Rāvaṇa.
t.7.26.8: Rāvaṇa, of exceedingly great valor, having fallen under the sway of the arrows of Kāma, sighed again and again and gazed at the moon.
t.7.26.7: Because of the singing and the abundance of flowers, because of the coolness of the wind and the charms of the mountain, and, as night had set in, by the rising of the moon,
t.7.26.9: Meanwhile, at that very place, Rambhā, foremost of all the Apsarases, adorned with celestial flowers and with a face like the full moon, appeared there.
t.7.26.10: Adorned with fresh, moist ornamental marks painted on her and with festive flowers of all six seasons, she was wrapped in a blue garment that looked like a rain-laden cloud.
t.7.26.11: She whose face was like the moon, whose lovely brows were like bows, whose thighs were shaped like an elephant's trunk and whose hands were soft as young shoots, was noticed by Rāvaṇa as she passed through the midst of the army.
t.7.26.12: The lord of the Rākṣasas, tormented by the force of Kāma's arrows, rose up, seized her by the hand as she was going, and, smiling, addressed her.
t.7.26.13: Where are you going, O lady of lovely hips? What fulfilment are you seeking of your own accord? Whose hour of good fortune is this, that he will enjoy you?
t.7.26.14: Who today will find his fill of the nectar of your mouth, fragrant with the scent of lotus and water-lily, like the very essence of ambrosial nectar?
t.7.26.15: O timid one, to whose chest will these breasts of yours, full, lovely, close together, and like golden pitchers, give their touch?
t.7.26.16: Who today will ascend that heaven of yours which takes the form of your hips, broad, resembling a golden wheel and adorned with strings of gold?
t.7.26.17: What other man is superior to me: Śakra, Viṣṇu, or the two Aśvins? Passing me by, timid one, to whom are you going? That is not becoming.
t.7.26.18: Rest here, O broad-hipped one; this stone slab is lovely. In the three worlds there is found no one, not even a lord, who is equal to me.
t.7.26.19: Therefore this Daśānana, bowing low with joined palms, entreats you: I, who am both the lord and the sustainer of the three worlds, ask you to accept me.
t.7.26.20: Thus addressed, Rambhā, trembling and with joined palms, said: "Be gracious! You ought not to speak such words, for you are my elder."
t.7.26.22: Daśagrīva said to her, who stood at his feet with her face bowed down: "If you are the wife of my son, then you would be my daughter-in-law."
t.7.26.21: Even from others I ought to be protected by you, should I ever suffer violation; and by dharma I am your daughter-in-law. I tell you this truth.
t.7.26.23: Saying, “So be it,” Rambhā gave Rāvaṇa this reply: “By dharma, O bull among Rākṣasas, I am the wife of your son.”
t.7.26.24: He who is renowned in the three worlds as Nalakūbara is the son of your brother Vaiśravaṇa, dearer to him than his own life-breaths.
t.7.26.26: I have indeed made a tryst with him, the son of the Lokapāla, and it is for his sake that all this adornment of mine has been put on.
t.7.26.25: He who in righteousness would be a brahmin and in valor a kṣatriya, who in wrath would be fire itself and in forbearance equal to the earth.
t.7.26.27: For it is his love, and no other's, that abides toward me; by that truth, O king, subduer of foes, you ought to release me.
t.7.26.28: For that righteous-souled one is waiting even now, eager for me; therefore you ought not to put an obstacle here in the way of your son. Release me!
t.7.26.29: Walk the path trodden by the virtuous, O bull among Rākṣasas; for you are to be honoured by me, and likewise I am to be cherished by you.
t.7.26.30: As Rambhā spoke these words in accord with dharma and artha, the mighty rākṣasa, in his delusion, rebuked her and seized her by force. Then, inflamed with lust and infatuation, he set about forcing himself upon her.
t.7.26.32: Trembling, ashamed and frightened, her hands joined in reverent salutation, she approached Nalakūbara and fell at his feet.
t.7.26.31: Then Rambhā, released, her garlands and ornaments fallen away, became as agitated as a river churned by the sport of a lordly elephant.
t.7.26.33: Seeing her in that state, the great-souled Nalakūbara said: "What is this, good lady, that you have fallen at my feet?"
t.7.26.34: But she, sighing and trembling, with her palms joined in supplication, began to tell him everything exactly as it had happened.
t.7.26.35: O lord, this Daśagrīva has arrived on his way to go to Triviṣṭapa, and the night is being spent here by him together with his army.
t.7.26.36: As I was coming to your presence, O subduer of foes, I was seen by him; seizing me, that Rākṣasa asked me, "To whom do you belong?"
t.7.26.37: Indeed, I told him all that was true, but his mind was overpowered by desire and delusion, and he did not listen to those words of mine.
t.7.26.38: Though I pleaded with him, O god, saying, “I am your daughter-in-law,” O lord, he cast all that aside, and by force I was violated by him.
t.7.26.39: Thus you ought to forgive me my offense, O giver of honor, for the strength of a woman and of a man is surely not equal, O gentle one.
t.7.26.40: Hearing this, the son of Vaiśravaṇa then became furious, and having heard of that grievous outrage, he sank deep into meditation.
t.7.26.41: Then, having learned of that deed of his, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, his eyes copper-red with rage, after a moment took water in his hand.
t.7.26.42: Taking up divine water and sipping it according to the prescribed rite, he then released a terrible curse upon the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.7.26.43: Since you, gentle lady, were forcibly violated by him against your will, he shall therefore never again approach any other young woman who does not desire him.
t.7.26.44: But when, tormented by desire, he violates a woman who is unwilling, then his head will shatter into seven pieces.
t.7.26.45: When that curse, blazing like a flaming fire, had been pronounced, the drums of the gods resounded, and a shower of flowers fell from the sky.
t.7.26.46: And all the gods, too, with Prajāpati at their head, rejoiced, knowing the entire course of the world and the death of that Rākṣasa.
t.7.26.47: Having heard that hair-raising curse, Daśagrīva no longer took pleasure in the thought of sexual union with women who were unwilling.
